tip: Formal 'Lei' commands use the subjunctive form, so 'lasciare' becomes 'lasci', not the informal 'lascia'.
'Senza che' takes the subjunctive and pairs with 'nessuno' where English says 'anyone': 'senza che nessuno se ne accorgesse'.
'Per la quale' is the formal written version of 'per cui', and 'la quale' agrees with the feminine 'azienda'.
In 'a meno che non ci sia' the 'non' is just part of the formula, not a real negation: it still means unless there is traffic.
'Il che' points back to the whole previous statement, not a single noun, which is why 'significa' follows it.
'Avendo' plus a past participle marks an action finished before the main verb: 'avendo finito il lavoro' = having finished work.
'Fare' plus an infinitive means to get something done by others. 'Ha fatto costruire una casa' = he had a house built, he did not build it himself.
'Purché' means 'provided that' and always takes the subjunctive: 'purché venga fatta giustizia' = as long as justice is done.
'Lungi' is an archaic 'far' that survives only in this formula: 'lungi dall'essere risolto' = far from being resolved.
'Il cui' means 'whose'. The article agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'il' matches 'figlio', not the 'donna' who owns it.
In 'ce la metto tutta' the 'ce' and 'la' are frozen bits of 'mettercela tutta'; the 'la' points at nothing specific.
'Fare' plus an infinitive means someone else does it for you: 'ho fatto riparare la macchina' = I had the car repaired.
'Farcela' means to manage or cope; here 'ce' and 'la' are fixed inside the verb and 'più' adds 'anymore': 'non ce la faccio più'.
'Prendersela' means to get upset or take it personally; add 'con' for the target: 'se la prende con me'.
A bare gerund covers English 'if' or 'by' with no separate word: 'andando avanti così' = if we go on like this.
'Foss'anche' means 'were it even'. It is 'fosse' (were) elided, and Italian drops 'se', so the inverted verb alone carries the 'even if'.
'Non fosse stato per te' means 'had it not been for you'. Italian drops 'se' and inverts the verb, just like formal English inverts 'had'.
'Sia come sia' is a frozen phrase, literally 'be it as it be'. Both verbs are the subjunctive 'sia', matching English 'be that as it may'.
In reported speech a future becomes the past conditional: 'arriverò' turns into 'sarebbe arrivato', never 'arriverebbe'.
'A prescindere da' means 'regardless of'. The open-ended 'ciò che' then pushes its verb into the subjunctive, hence 'abbiano deciso'.
With no 'se' in front, 'avesse almeno avuto' means 'if only he had had'; this bare subjunctive voices regret.
'Pur essendo stanco' means 'despite being tired'. 'Pur' plus a gerund packs a whole 'although' clause into just two words.
'Quale che sia' is a literary, formal way to say 'whichever it may be'; the verb 'sia' is present subjunctive.
